page.title: Turntable With Built-In Preamp: Line Output Compared
page.h1: Turntable with a built-in preamp: which one drives powered speakers hardest
page.desc: Built-in phono preamps compared by line output: Audio-Technica AT-LP70X at 252 mV vs Fluance RT80, RT81 and RT81+ at 140 mV. The figures, the arithmetic and our pick.
page.answer: Short answer. The best turntable with a built-in phono preamp in 2026 is the Audio-Technica AT-LP70X: set to LINE, its preamp lifts the 4 mV cartridge signal to 252 mV, about 5 dB louder than the Fluance RT81's 140 mV, so powered speakers need less volume.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Line level: 20·log10(252 ÷ 140) = 5.1 dB. At the same volume setting, the AT-LP70X and AT-LP70XBT play about 5 dB louder than any of the three Fluance decks.
  • Audio-Technica's preamp checks out: 4.0 mV × 10^(36/20) = 4.0 × 63.1 = 252 mV, which matches the line level Audio-Technica states.
  • Fluance's gain, worked out from its own figures: 20·log10(140 ÷ 3.5) = 32.0 dB for the RT80 and RT81, and 20·log10(140 ÷ 4.0) = 30.9 dB for the RT81+. Fluance gives the same 140 mV for the RT81+ even though its cartridge is 20·log10(4.0 ÷ 3.5) = 1.2 dB hotter.
  • RT81+ over RT81: $349.99 − $299.99 = $50. The extra buys the AT-VM95E cartridge, an acrylic mat and adjustable feet, not more output.
  • Stylus running cost on the Fluance decks: the ATN95E and AT-VMN95E both cost $52.99 at Fluance. That works out to $52.99 ÷ 500 h = $0.11 per hour up to $52.99 ÷ 300 h = $0.18 per hour.
Your setupFits

Manual deck on the tightest budgetFluance RT80, $249.99, with a conical stylus per its spec table

How the built-in preamp sets your volume

A cartridge puts out only a few millivolts: 4.0 mV for Audio-Technica's AT-VM95C and 3.5 mV for Fluance's AT95E. The built-in preamp applies the RIAA curve and the gain that lift this to line level. Fluance's instructions are to slide the switch to LINE for powered speakers or an amplifier without a phono input, and to PHONO when using an external preamp, which bypasses all of the deck's electronics. Audio-Technica says the AT-LP70XBT's line output is fixed at 252 mV with a 4.0 mV cartridge, with no volume control on the deck. Your speakers' volume knob does all the adjusting.

That 140 mV has drawn criticism before. In his RT81 review for SECRETS of Home Theater and High Fidelity, John E. Johnson, Jr. listed "higher output (0.5 volts) from the phono preamplifier" as an improvement he wanted. By the arithmetic, 20·log10(500 ÷ 140) = 11.1 dB short of that target, while the AT-LP70X falls 20·log10(500 ÷ 252) = 6.0 dB short. The Fluance decks have their own strengths: a true preamp bypass, and an A-weighted ≥ 67 dB S/N figure, where Audio-Technica gives > 55 dB without naming a weighting. The RT81+ is also the only deck here with a named third-party speed check: Thom Moon at SoundStage! Access read 33.5 rpm at 33⅓ (about 0.55% fast) with ±0.17% wow, using a phone app. Fluance's tonearm takes 3.5–6.5 g cartridges, works with the Ortofon 2M Red and does not work with the 2M Blue (Fluance support).

Not recommended

Fluance RT82, if you need a preamp. Fluance prices it at $349.99, the same as the RT81+, but its own comparison table lists no built-in preamp. It cannot drive powered speakers directly. Fluance RT81 over the RT81+. It has the same 140 mV preamp stage for $50 less, but it ships the older AT95E. Fluance's upgrade route for the RT81 is a whole new AT-VM95 cartridge, while the RT81+'s VM95E already takes every VM95 stylus.
